props.description: A form of stress fractures that result when normal force is applied to bones with deficient elasticity.

props.name: diaphyseal fracture
props.description: A fracture along the shaft of a long bone.

props.name: intercondylar fracture
props.description: A longitudinal fracture of the humerus between its two condyles.

props.name: complete fracture
props.description: A fracture involving the entire cross section of the bone.

props.name: loose body
props.description: A small piece of bone or cartilage within a joint, usually the result of wear and tear and/or trauma.

props.name: bone marrow oedema
props.description: A condition in which the bone marrow takes on an excessive amount of fluid.

props.name: cyst
props.description: A sac-like closed membranous structure that may be empty or contain fluid or amorphous material.

props.name: subchondral cyst
props.description: A bone cyst within the fused epiphysis beneath the articular plate.

props.name: synovial plica syndrome
props.description: A condition which occurs when a synovial plica becomes irritated, enlarged or inflamed.

props.name: cartilage disease
props.description: A condition in which there is a deviation from or interruption of the normal structure or function of cartilage.

props.name: cartilage loss
props.description: Articular cartilage does not usually regenerate after injury or disease leading to loss of tissue and formation of a defect.

props.name: cartilage flap
props.description: Cartilage separates from the bone and moves.

props.name: fissure
props.description: Fissuring represents disruption at right angle to the surface, and may extend to partial or full thickness.

props.name: irregularity
props.description: Marked deviation from normal.

props.name: arthropathy
props.description: A disease or an abnormality of a joint.

props.name: effusion
props.description: A collection of fluid in a body cavity.

props.name: joint effusion

props.name: Horizontal ipsilateral gaze palsy
props.description:
Horizontal-gaze abnormalities are more common than vertical ones. Because the horizontal-gaze system depends on unilateral gaze centers and pathways, it is more vulnerable than the vertical-gaze system, which has bilateral input. Horizontal-gaze paresis can vary from (a) gaze-evoked nystagmus to (b) slowing or dysmetria of the movement to (c) a total inability to move the eyes in the involved direction of gaze. Severe gaze paralysis results in conjugate deviation of the eyes in the opposite direction at rest.
The most common abnormalities in this group are gaze palsies resulting from a cerebrovascular accident (CVA). Localization of the lesion depends on concurrent neurologic findings such as hemiparesis, visual field loss, and cranial nerve palsies. The following discussion covers saccade abnormalities first and then pursuit abnormalities.
An isolated horizontal-gaze paresis is rare. The lesion can be located anywhere in the horizontal-gaze pathways and cannot be localized more specifically without other neurologic signs and symptoms.

props.name: vertigo
props.description: Vertigo is an unpleasant distortion of static gravitational orientation or an erroneous perception of motion of either the sufferer or the environment. It is not a well-defined disease entity, but rather the outcome of many pathological processes causing a mismatch between the visual, vestibular, and somatosensory systems, all of which subserve both static and dynamic spatial orientation. Physiological and clinical vestibular vertigo syndromes are commonly characterized by a combination of phenomena involving perceptual, ocular motor, postural and vegetative manifestations: vertigo, nystagmus, ataxia and nausea. The vertigo itself results from a disturbance of cortical spatial orientation, while nystagmus and ocular deviations are secondary to a direction-specific imbalance in the vestibulo-ocular reflex. Postural imbalance and vestibular ataxia are caused by inappropriate or abnormal inactivation of vestibulospinal pathways. Unpleasant vegetative effects, such as nausea and vomiting, are related to clinical activation of the medullary vomiting centre

props.name: Thalamic infarction syndrome
props.description:
The thalamus is a centrally situated structure with extensive reciprocal connections with the cortex, basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei. Therefore it can mimic cortical and subcortical strokes in the anterior or posterior circulation and is also called “the great imitator”. Its vascularization is subdivided into four territories correlated with the organization of the thalamic nuclei:
- the tuberothalamic (or polar) artery
-the thalamogeniculate (or inferolateral) artery
-the paramedian arteries
-the posterior choroidal artery (PChA).

props.name: Hemiballismus
props.description:
Hemiballism is a rare hyperkinetic movement disorder, characterized by irregular, wide amplitude and vigorous involuntary movements of the unilateral limbs. The term ballismus is derived from the Greek word meaning "to throw" because the abnormal movements resemble the motions of throwing. The movements are usually continuous but may be intermittent and can be voluntarily restrained by the patient, although only for a few minutes. They are most prominent during periods of rest but are absent during sleep. It may occur with other types of involuntary movements, such as dystonia, myoclonus, or orofacial gestures. Hemiballism is often used interchangeably but distinguished from hemichorea by the fact that hemichoreic movements are slower, more randomly distributed, less violent, and primarily involve distal musculature. Some patients with hemiballism also have choreiform movements; therefore, the bhemiballism-hemichoreaQ is often used to
describe this clinical spectrum.

props.description: Start position: Stand upright with feet shoulder width apart. Action: Without using hands bend the knees, hips and trunk to lower down towards the chair. Before sitting down rise back to the start position. Repeat.

props.name: single leg balance on uneven or unstable surface
props.description: Start position: Stand on uneven or unstable surface (e.g. grass, soft mat, trampoline, balance cushion, wobble board, soft carpet, sand, etc.) and balance on the affected leg. Action: Maintain balance on the affected leg without using your arms or the unaffected leg for support.

props.name: single leg balance with ball catching
props.description: Start position: Balance on the affected leg. Action: Maintain balance on the affected leg without using your arms or the unaffected leg for support and throw and catch a ball. Variations: standing on an uneven or unstable surface.

props.name: single leg balance with closed eyes
props.description: Start position: Balance on the affected leg. Action: Maintain balance on the affected leg, shut eyes and keep balance without using your arms or the unaffected leg for support. Variations: standing on an uneven or unstable surface.

props.name: vertical hopping
props.description: Start position: Stand on the affected leg. Action: Bend the affected knee, hop upwards, land and keep your balance on the affected leg. Variations: on an uneven or unstable surface; catching and throwing a ball, increasing hop height; increasing knee bend.

props.name: single leg lateral hopping
props.description: Start position: Stand on the affected leg. Action: Slightly bend the affected knee and hop to the side landing on the same leg allowing the knee to bend. Keep the balance and hop back to the start position. Variations: catching and throwing a ball; Increasing the hopping distance.

props.name: hopping for distance
props.description: Start position: Stand on the affected leg. Action: Bend the affected knee, hop forwards and land keeping balance on the affected leg. Repeat. Variations: increasing hop distance.

props.name: crossover hopping
props.description: Start position: Stand on the affected leg. Action: Bend the affected knee, hop diagonally and land keeping balance on the affected leg. Hop diagonally in the other direction. Variations: catching and throwing a ball; increasing hop distance; performing on an uneven surface; increasing hop speed.

props.name: hopping up steps
props.description: Start position: Stand on the affected leg in front of the step. Action: Bend the affected knee, hop up onto the step and land keeping balance on the affected leg. Variations: catching and throwing a ball.

props.name: vertical jumping
props.description: Start position: Stand upright. Action: Bend the knees, jump upwards and land with equal weight on both legs. Variations: on an uneven or unstable surface; catching and throwing a ball; increasing height; increasing knee bend; altering trunk position.

props.name: lateral jumping
props.description: Start position: Stand upright. Action: Bend the knees, jump sideways and land with equal weight on both legs. Jump sideways in the other direction. Variations: on an uneven or unstable surface; catching and throwing a ball; increasing height; increasing knee bend; altering trunk position.

props.name: jumping for distance
props.description: Start position: Stand upright. Action: Bend the knees, jump forwards and land with equal weight on both legs. Variations: on an uneven or unstable surface; catching and throwing a ball; increasing distance; increasing height; increasing knee bend; altering trunk position.

props.name: jumping up steps
props.description: Start position: Stand upright in front of the step. Action: Bend the knees, jump up onto the step and land with equal weight on both legs. Variations: catching and throwing a ball; altering trunk position.

props.name: squat jumping
props.description: Start position: Stand upright. Action: Squat then jump up as high as possible and land with equal weight on both legs. Variations: catching and throwing a ball; altering trunk position.

props.name: sport-specific exercise
props.description: Sport-specific exercise is an exercise consisting of movements that are specific to a particular sport.

props.name: pilates
props.description: A body conditioning routine that may help build flexibility, muscle strength, and endurance in the legs, abdominals, arms, hips, and back. It puts emphasis on spinal and pelvic alignment, breathing, and developing a strong core or center, and improving coordination and balance.

props.name: yoga
props.description: Exercises designed to tone, strengthen and align the body through postures performed to make the spine supple and healthy and to promote blood flow to all the organs, glands, and tissues.

props.name: mini squats
props.description: Start position: Stand upright with feet shoulder width apart. Action: Slowly bend knees until the knees are flexed 45 degrees, then slowly straighten knees back to the start position.

props.name: single leg squats
props.description: Start position: Stand on the affected leg. Action: Bend the knee over the foot as low as is comfortable without losing balance, then slowly straighten the affected knee back to the start position. Variations: adding hand weights; adding calf raises when rising from the squat; on an uneven or unstable surface; throwing a ball at a target; adding upper body movements; extending the contralateral leg with or without elastic resistance.

props.name: wall squats
props.description: Start position: Stand upright with the back supported against a wall and feet shoulder width apart. Action: Slowly bend knees and slide down the wall until the thighs are parallel to the floor, then slowly straighten knees back to the start position.

props.name: diagnostic procedure
props.description: A procedure, method, or technique used to determine the nature or identity of a disease or disorder. This excludes procedures which are primarily carried out on specimens in a laboratory.

props.name: valgus stress test
props.description: Patient supine on the examination table. Flex the knee to 30 degrees over the side of the table, place one hand about the lateral aspect of the knee, and grasp the ankle with the other hand. Apply abduction (valgus) stress to the knee. The test must also be performed in full extension.

props.name: varus stress test
props.description: Patient supine on the examination table. Flex the knee to 30 degrees over the side of the table, place one hand about the medial aspect of the knee, and grasp the ankle with the other hand. Apply adduction (varus) stress to the knee. The test must also be performed in full extension.

props.name: Apley grind test
props.description: A test for a meniscal injury. The patient is prone with the knee flexed at 90 degrees. The examiner grasps the foot with both hands and externally rotates it as far as possible while pushing down though the tibia. When this limit is reached, the examiner rotates the foot internally. Increased pain during rotation indicates a positive test.

props.name: Apley distraction test
props.description: The patient is prone with the knee flexed at 90 degrees. The examiner grasps the foot with both hands and externally rotates it as far as possible while pulling the tibia upwards. When this limit is reached, the examiner rotates the foot internally. Increased pain during rotation indicates a positive test.

props.name: Ege's test
props.description: A test for a meniscal injury. The patient starts in a standing position with the knees fully extended and the feet 30cm apart. If testing the medial meniscus, the feet will be fully externally rotated. If testing the lateral meniscus, the feet will be internally rotated. The patient then squats and then slowly stands up to return to the starting position. The test is positive when pain and/or a click is felt by the patient at the related site of the joint line.

props.name: lateral pull test
props.description: Patient supine with toes pointing upwards. The patient is asked to perform an isometric contraction of quadriceps femoris muscle against the table. The tracking of the patella is graded. The patella should be pulled in a straight superior direction or superior and lateral in equal proportions. If the patella tracks more laterally than superiorly, then the test is positive.

props.name: passive patellar tilt test
props.description: A test for assessing patellar laxity. The patient lies supine. The examiner lifts the lateral edge of patella from the lateral femoral condyle avoiding lateral subluxation. Normally the patella lies parallel to the horizontal or the outer edge may be slightly tilted up (less than 10 degrees). A neutral or negative angle indicates excessively tight lateral restraint. A high positive angle indicates deficiencies of the lateral constraints.

props.name: Anderson grind test
props.description: A test for a meniscal injury. The test is performed with the patient supine and the leg cradled between the examiner's trunk and arm while the index finger and thumb of the opposite hand are placed over the anterior joint line. A valgus stress is applied to the knee as it is passively flexed to 45 degrees; then a varus stress is applied to the knee as it is passively extended, producing a circular motion to the knee. The motion is repeated, increasing the varus and valgus stresses with each rotation of the knee. Positive result is 'grinding' sensation felt with examiner's hand.

props.name: Passler rotational grind test
props.description: A test for a meniscal injury. The patient is seated. The examiner immobilizes the foot of the affected leg. The examiner palpates the medial joint line and moves the patient's knee in a circle with tibial rotation. At the same time, the examiner applies a varus or valgus stress. Pain increased with the circular motion indicates a positive test.

props.name: Payr test
props.description: A test for a meniscal injury. The patient is sitting with legs crossed. The examiner exerts downward pressure along the medial aspect of the affected knee. Medial knee pain indicates a positive test, usually a lesion of the posterior horn.

props.name: anterior drawer test
props.description: The subject is supine, hip flexed to 45 degrees and knee flexed to 90 degrees. Examiner sits on the subject's foot, with hands behind the proximal tibia and thumbs on the tibial plateau. Anterior force applied to the proximal tibia. Hamstring tendons palpated with index fingers to ensure relaxation. Increased tibial displacement compared with the opposite side is indicative of an ACL tear.

props.name: posterior drawer test
props.description: Subject is supine with the test hip flexed to 45 degrees, knee flexed to 90 degrees, and foot in a neutral position. The examiner is sitting on the subject's foot with both hands behind the subject's proximal tibia and thumbs on the tibial plateau. Apply a posterior force to the proximal tibia. Increased posterior tibial displacement as compared with the uninvolved side is indicative of a partial or complete tear of the PCL.

props.name: posterior sag test
props.description: Patient lies supine with the hip flexed to 45 degrees and the knee flexed to 90 degrees. In this position, the tibia rocks back, or sags back, on the femur if the PCL is torn. Normally, the medial tibial plateau extends 1cm anteriorly beyond the femoral condyle when the knee is flexed 90 degrees. If this step-off is lost, the step-off test is considered positive.

props.name: quadriceps active test
props.description: Subject is supine with knee flexed to 90 degrees in the drawer-test position. The foot is stabilized by the examiner, and the subject is asked to slide the foot gently down the table. Contraction of the quadriceps muscle in the PCL-deficient knee results in an anterior shift of the tibia of not less than 2mm. The test is qualitative.

props.name: Lachman test
props.description: Patient lies supine. Knee held between full extension and 15 degrees of flexion. Femur is stabilized with one hand while firm pressure is applied to the posterior aspect of the proximal tibia in an attempt to translate it anteriorly. Test is positive (indicating ACL rupture) when there is anterior translation of the tibia with 'soft' endpoint.

props.name: reverse Lachman test
props.description: A test for posterior instability. The patient lies supine and the knee flexed to 20-30 degrees. The examiner draws the tibia posteriorly relative to the femur. The excessive magnitude of tibial motion compared to the uninjured knee together with a soft end feel indicates a positive test.

props.name: Loomer test
props.description: A test for knee posterolateral instability, which is a modification of the standard posterolateral rotatory instability test, is described. In this test, the patient lies supine on the examination table with hips and knees flexed to 90 degrees. The examiner grasps both feet and attempts to maximally externally rotate them. A positive test is indicated by (1) excessive external rotation of the affected tibia, which is easily recognized since the feet act as pointers and amplify the external rotation, and (2) a slight posterior sag of the affected tibial tubercle, which is more subtle but still a very recognizable sign.

props.name: Hughston plica test
props.description: A test for a synovial plica syndrome. The patient is supine. The examiner flexes the knee with medial rotation of the tibia and pressing the patella medially while palpating just medial to the patella. A snapping and/or popping felt and/or heard indicates a positive test.

props.name: Losee test
props.description: The patient lies supine on the examination table. The examiner supports the involved side ankle with one hand. The tibia is externally rotated. The patient's knee is then flexed to approximately 45 degrees. The examiner places his other hand on the lateral side of the knee. The thumb is hooked behind the fibular head and the fingers are placed over the patella. This hand then applies a valgus force to the knee while the thumb lifts upward on the fibular head, internally rotating the tibia. The knee is slowly extended while the valgus force is being applied. The leg and foot are allowed to roll into internal rotation. If the test is positive, the lateral tibial plateau will suddenly subluxate anteriorly as the knee reaches approximately 10-20 degrees of flexion.

props.name: Martens test
props.description: The patient is supine on the table with the knee held at 30 degrees of flexion. The lower limb is braced against the abdomen of the examiner. While giving a lateral thrust on the tibia using the elbow of the examiner at the foot of the patient and a concomitant internal rotation of the tibia by an endotorsion of the hand placed upon the tibia one carries out the same downwards movement on the femur and upwards pushing of the tibia to evaluate anterolateral instability. A sudden snap of varying degree can easily be felt and seen in case of anterior subluxation of the lateral tibial plateau.

props.name: Slocum test
props.description: A test for anteromedial rotary instability and anterolateral rotary instability of the knee. The patient is supine with the knee flexed 90 degrees and the foot fixed to the examining table by the examiner. 30 degrees of internal rotation is applied to the tibia by rotating the foot. The examiner pulls anteriorly on the tibia to assess for anterolateral rotary instability. Results are compared bilaterally. Increased amount of anterior tibial translation with tibial internal rotation or excessive movement on the lateral aspect of the knee indicates anterolateral instability. To examine anteromedial rotary instability the tibia is laterally rotated 15 degrees and the tibia is once again pulled forward. Results are compared bilaterally. When pathologically increased forward and outward displacement of the tibia on the femur is possible, excessive anterior rotation of the medial tibial plateau indicates laxity of the medial structures.

props.name: DeJour test
props.description: A test for anterolateral rotary instability of knee. The patient lies supine. The examiner immobilises the foot by wedging it between the body and the elbow. The examiner places one hand flat under the patient's tibia, pushing it forwards with the knee in extension. The other hand is placed against the patient's thigh, pushing the other way. The lower limb is taken into slight abduction by the examiner's elbow, with the examiner's body acting as a fulcrum to produce the valgus force. The examiner maintains the anterior tibial translation and the valgus force while flexing the knee. At 20-30 degrees of flexion, a positive test is indicated if pivot shift occurs with a clunk as the lateral tibial plateau suddenly reduces.

props.name: McMurray test
props.description: With the patient lying flat, the knee is first fully flexed; the foot is held by grasping the heel. The leg is rotated on the thigh with the knee still in full flexion. By altering the position of flexion, the whole of the posterior segment of the cartilages can be examined from the middle to their posterior attachment. Bring the leg from its position of acute flexion to a right angle while the foot is retained first in full internal rotation and then in full external rotation. When the click occurs (in association with a torn meniscus), the patient is able to state that the sensation is the same as he/she experienced when the knee gave way previously.

props.name: bounce home test
props.description: The test is performed with the patient supine and the foot cupped in the examiner's hand. With the patient's knee completely flexed, the knee is passively allowed to extend. The knee should extend completely or bounce home into extension with a sharp endpoint. If extension is not complete or has a rubbery end feel, there is probably a torn meniscus or some other blockage.

props.name: McConnell test
props.description: A test for chondromalacia patellae. The patient is seated with the femur externally rotated and knee flexed to 120 degrees. The patient then performs a 10-second isometric contraction. If pain is experienced during the contraction, the knee is passively extended and then a medial glide applied to the patella. The knee is returned to the position that caused pain, and the patient again performs an isometric contraction while the medial patella glide is maintained. If the pain experienced is decreased, chondromalacia patellae is suspected. The test is repeated with the knee at various flexion angles.

props.name: O'Donoghue test
props.description: A test for a meniscal injury or capsular irritation. The patient is prone. The examiner flexes the knee to 90 degrees, rotates the tibia internally and externally twice, and then fully extends the knee. The process is repeated. Increased pain during rotation indicates a positive test.

props.name: patellar apprehension test
props.description: A test for patellar dislocation. The subject is supine and relaxed. The examiner pushes the patella as lateral as possible. Then the examiner flexes the knee flexed to 30 degrees and sustains the lateral glide. The subject's apprehension indicates a positive test.

props.name: Wilson test
props.description: A test used to detect the presence of Osteochondritis dissecans of the knee. The patient is sitting on a table with legs dangling over the edge. The examiner bends the patient's knee so that it is flexed at a 90 degrees angle, then grasps the patient's foot and brings the tibia in (internal rotation). The patient is asked to extend the leg until the pain is felt. The test is positive if the patient reports pain in the knee about 30 degrees from full extension and when by rotating the foot back (external rotation of the tibia) in its normal position the pain disappears.

props.name: Thessaly test
props.description: The Thessaly test is a dynamic reproduction of joint loading in the knee. The test is performed at 5 degrees and 20 degrees of flexion. The examiner supports the patient by holding their outstretched hands while the patient stands flatfooted on the floor. The patient then rotates his or her knee and body, internally and externally, three times, keeping the knee in slight flexion (5 degrees). The same procedure is then carried out with the knee flexed at 20 degrees. Patients with suspected meniscal tears experience medial or lateral joint line discomfort and may have a sense of locking or catching.

props.name: Noble test
props.description: A provocative test of the iliotibial band. It is commonly used as an indication for iliotibial band syndrome. The subject is supine. Bring the affected knee up to a 90 degree flexion and apply pressure with a thumb to the lateral femoral epicondyle. Afterwards the leg is extended slowly. When it is extended at approximately 30 degrees, the iliotibial band translates anteriorly over the lateral femoral epicondyle under the examiners thumb. If the patient indicates pain at this 30 degree angle, which is similar to when the patient is active, then the test is positive.

props.name: Steinmann first test
props.description: The patient is supine. The knee is held flexed at 90 degrees and forced to external rotation, then internal rotation. The test is positive for medial meniscal tear if raises pain upon externally rotating, while it is positive for lateral meniscal tears in case of pain during internal rotation.

props.name: Steinmann second test
props.description: In Steinmann's second test joint line tenderness migrates posteriorly with knee flexion and anteriorly with knee extension, following the movements of the meniscus. To perform a meniscal stress manoeuvre, the knee is held in Cabot's position and then the knee swings rapidly from a varus to a valgus stress, while a finger is pushed in the joint line. This brings the meniscus toward the periphery of the joint while the finger pushes it toward the centre of the joint: the combination of these two opposite forces stresses the meniscus, raising a sharp pain in case of meniscal tear.

props.name: Waldron test
props.description: A two-phase test for patellofemoral pain syndrome. For phase I, the subject is supine and the examiner presses the patella against the femur while simultaneously performing a passive knee flexion with the other hand. Crepitus and pain during a particular part of the range of motion are considered signs of patellofemoral pain disorders. For phase II, the subject is standing and asked to perform a slow, full squat, again with the examiner performing a gentle compression of the patella against the femur. Crepitus and pain indicate a positive test.

props.name: pivot shift test
props.description: Leg picked up at the ankle; the knee is flexed by placing the heel of the hand behind the fibula. As the knee is extended, the tibia is supported on the lateral side with a slight valgus strain. A strong valgus force is placed on the knee by the upper hand. At approximately 30 degrees of flexion, the displaced tibia will suddenly reduce, indicating a positive pivot shift test.

props.name: reverse pivot shift test
props.description: A test for posterolateral rotary instability. The patient lies supine with their knee flexed to between 45 and 60 degrees and their foot externally rotated. The examiner applies a valgus force while slowly extending the knee. A clunk will be felt around 30 degrees of knee flexion if the subluxed or dislocated joint has reduced. Boh knees are always tested for comparison in order to avoid false positives.

props.name: classification
props.description: A term or system of terms denoting an arrangement by class or category.

props.name: Orchard Sports Injury Classification System - Version 10
props.description: The OSICS-10 is an injury classification system that supports classification of diagnoses for summary studies.

props.name: knee injuries
props.description: Injuries to the knee or the knee joint.

props.name: complication of knee laceration/abrasion incl infection
patellar tendinopathy (excl. Sinding Larsen Johannson syndrome see JTKP)
insertional patellar tendon pathology, incl. intratend ossicle (excl. Osgoode Schlatters - see JTKT)
medial hamstring tendinopathy, incl. pes anserine bursitis
isolated ACL strain/rupture with chondral/meniscal injury
PCL strain/rupture with associated chondral/meniscal injury
MCL strain/rupture with chondral/meniscal damage knee
complication post MCL strain/rupture incl Pellegrini Steida lesion
posterolateral corner and LCL ligament injuries knee
combined ligament injury with chondral/meniscal injury
knee cartilage injury (chondral/osteochondral/meniscal) - excl. chondral inj a/w major ligament injury see KJXX
knee osteochondral injury (excl. osteochondritis dessicans i.e. atraumatic lesion - see JCKS)
two or more osteochondral injury sites
knee cartilage injury with loose bodies
patellar dislocation with avulsion fracture patella
knee dislocation with neural or vascular complication
knee impingement/synovitis/biomechanical Lesion not associated with other conditions
diagnostic imaging
props.description: Any method that uses a visual display of structural or functional patterns of organs or tissues for diagnostic evaluation.

props.name: magnetic resonance imaging
props.description: Imaging that uses radiofrequency waves and a strong magnetic field rather than x-rays to provide amazingly clear and detailed pictures of internal organs and tissues. The technique is valuable for the diagnosis of many pathologic conditions, including cancer, heart and vascular disease, stroke, and joint and musculoskeletal disorders.

props.name: radiography
props.description: A radiographic procedure using the emission of x-rays to form an image of the structure penetrated by the radiation.

props.name: ultrasonography
props.description: A technique in which high-frequency sound waves are bounced off internal organs and the echo pattern is converted into a 2 dimensional picture of the structures beneath the transducer.

props.name: X-ray computed tomography
props.description: A method of examining body organs by scanning them with X rays and using a computer to construct a series of cross-sectional scans along a single axis.

props.name: manual muscle test
props.description: A test to determine a patient's ability to voluntarily contract a specific muscle or a group of muscles. Patient Is asked to hold a position against examiner's resistance.

props.name: FITT activity level
props.description: The FITT (Frequency-Intensity-Time-Type) activity level is determined by how often, how hard, how long, and what kinds of activity one performs to support health and fitness.

props.name: FITT activity level 0
props.description: No moderate or vigorous activity of 20 minutes duration.

props.name: FITT activity level 1
props.description: 1-4 occasions of a mix of moderate and vigorous activity in 4 weeks.

props.name: FITT activity level 2
props.description: 5-11 occasions of a mix of moderate and vigorous activity in 4 weeks.

props.name: FITT activity level 3
props.description: 12 or more occasions of a moderate activity in 4 weeks.

props.name: FITT activity level 4
props.description: 12 or more occasions of a mix of moderate and vigorous activity in 4 weeks.

props.name: FITT activity level 5
props.description: 12 or more occasions of vigorous activity in 4 weeks.

props.name: MRC grade - muscle power
props.description: A scale for grading muscle power in stages from 0 to 5.

props.name: MRC grade - muscle power 0
props.description: No active muscle contraction.

props.name: MRC grade - muscle power 1
props.description: Visible muscle contraction only.

props.name: MRC grade - muscle power 2
props.description: Movement with gravity eliminated.

props.name: MRC grade - muscle power 3
props.description: Movement against gravity.

props.name: MRC grade - muscle power 4
props.description: Muscle movement against resistance incomplete.

props.name: MRC grade - muscle power 5
props.description: Movement against resistance.

props.name: muscle acting on joint
props.description: A skeletal muscle whose contraction supports joint movement.

props.name: sweep test
props.description: A test for joint effusion in the knee area. The patient lies in supine with the knee in full extension and relaxed. The examiner sweeps their hand upwards 2 or 3 times from beneath the medial tibiofemoral joint line towards the supra patellar bursa.  The examiner then strokes downwards on the lateral aspect of the knee, superior to the suprapatellar bursa towards the lateral joint line. The test is positive if a small bulge is detected on the medial aspect of the knee inferior to the patella.

props.name: patellar tap
props.description: A test for joint effusion in the knee area. The patient lies supine with the leg extended. The examiner puts pressure on the proximal side of the knee to squeeze the fluid out of the suprapatellar pouch. While maintaining pressure on the suprapatellar pouch the other hand presses up on the medial and lateral recesses. Tap down the patella with the index finger to create an upward and downward movement and a palpable 'click' as the patella hits the underlying femur. The test is positive if the patella can be felt to move down through the fluid. If the femur and the patella are already in contact, the test is negative. Both knees are always tested for comparison in order to avoid false positives.

props.name: Hoffa test
props.description: A test for a fat pad impingement. The patient is supine with their knees bent. The examiner presses both thumbs deeply along the sides of the patellar tendon just below the patella. The patient is then instructed to straighten the leg. Pain and/or apprehension of the patient indicate a positive test.

props.name: Clarke test
props.description: A test for patellofemoral pain syndrome. The subject is supine and relaxed with both knees supported by a knee pad. The examiner presses the patella distally and then asks the subject to contract the quadriceps muscle. The pain indicates positive test.

props.name: muscle quality
props.description: A quality that inheres in a muscle.

props.name: clinical measurement
props.description: An observable or measurable property or state of an organism of clinical interest.

props.name: body morphological measurement
props.description: Measurement of the structure or forms of the entire body or parts of the body of an organism.

props.name: cardiovascular measurement
props.description: A measurement to assess the morphological or physiological state of the cardiovascular system or portion of the cardiovascular system.

props.name: blood pressure measurement
props.description: Measurement of the pressure, or force per area, exerted by circulating blood against the walls of the blood vessels. The pressure is dependent on the energy of the heart action, elasticity of the vessel walls and volume and viscosity of the blood.

props.name: diastolic blood pressure
props.description: The minimum arterial pressure within the cardiac cycle, usually at the point at which the heart is in a state of relaxation and expansion. This is the time when the ventricles fill with blood.

props.name: systolic blood pressure
props.description: The maximum arterial pressure within the cardiac cycle, i.e. at the point at which the heart is in its maximal state of contraction. This is the time when the blood is forced from the ventricles of the heart into the pulmonary artery and the aorta.

props.name: heart rate
props.description: The number of heartbeats per unit of time, usually expressed as beats per minute.

props.name: pulse rate
props.description: The count of the rhythmic contractions and expansions of an artery due to the surge of blood from the beat of the heart.

props.name: musculoskeletal system measurement
props.description: Measurement of the bodily system that consists of the muscles, bones, joints, and related structures, such as the tendons and connective tissue and which supports and protects the body, functions in the movement of body parts and organs, produces blood cells, and stores minerals.

props.name: joint measurement
props.description: Measurement of one or more of the articulations between bones which may be immovable, slightly movable or freely movable.

props.name: muscle measurement
props.description: Any measurement, morphological or physiological of a muscle or a group of muscles. Muscles are organs or tissues composed of bundles of fibers that have the power to contract and hence to produce movement.

props.name: respiratory system measurement
props.description: A measurement to assess the morphological or physiological state of the respiratory system or portion of the respiratory system.

props.name: forced expiratory volume
props.description: Fraction of forced vital capacity that is exhaled in a specific number of seconds.

props.name: forced expiratory volume to forced vital capacity ratio
props.description: The comparison of forced expiratory volume to forced vital capacity expressed as ratio or percentage.

props.name: forced vital capacity
props.description: The volume of air that can be forcibly expelled from a maximally inflated lung.

props.name: maximal carbon dioxide production
props.description: The rate of elimination of carbon dioxide from the lungs.

props.name: maximal oxygen consumption
props.description: Maximum capacity of an individual's body to transport and utilize oxygen, usually measured during exercise as volume of oxygen per unit of time.

props.name: total lung capacity
props.description: Total volume to which lungs can be expanded with greatest inspiratory effort.

props.name: residual lung volume
props.description: The amount of gas remaining in the lung at the end of a maximal exhalation.

props.name: maximum mid-expiratory flow
props.description: Maximal rate of air flow through the pulmonary tree during forced expiration.

props.name: Q angle
props.description: The Q angle is the angle of incidence of the quadriceps muscle relative to the patella. It determines the tracking of the patella through the trochlea of the femur.

props.name: anatomical abnormality
props.description: An abnormal structure, or one that is abnormal in size or location.

props.name: ligamentous laxity
props.description: Ligamentous laxity is a term given to describe 'loose ligaments'.

props.name: abnormality of the knee
props.description: An abnormality of the knee joint or surrounding structures.

props.name: bipartite patella
props.description: A developmental defect that occurs if the two halves of the patella fail to fuse in early childhood.

props.name: abnormality of the patella
props.description: Abnormality of the patella (knee cap).

props.name: flat feet
props.description: A foot where the 'plantar arch' (FMA:43942) is in contact with the ground or floor when the individual is standing; or, in a patient lying supine, a foot where the arch is in contact with the surface of a flat board pressed against the sole of the foot by the examiner with a pressure similar to that expected from weight bearing; or, the height of the arch is reduced.

props.name: tibial torsion
props.description: Tibial torsion is inward twisting ('medial roation') (PATO:0002155) of the 'tibia' (FMA:24476).

props.name: femoral retroversion
props.description: Femoral retroversion is an excessive external hip rotation.

props.name: femoral anteversion
props.description: Femoral anteversion is an excessive internal hip rotation.

props.name: genu varum

props.name: genu valgum
props.description: The legs angle inward, such that the knees are close together and the ankles far apart.

props.name: genu recurvatum
props.description: The backward curvature of the knee; hyperextension of the knee.

props.name: knee flexion contracture
props.description: A bent (flexed) knee joint that cannot be straightened actively or passively.

props.name: physical examination

props.name: performance test
props.description: Tests requiring nonverbal responses, for example, the manipulation of objects or the performance of motor skills.

props.name: test finding
props.description: The result of a laboratory, radiologic, or other clinical test performed to determine the presence, absence, or degree of a condition.

props.name: positive finding
props.description: An observation confirming something, such as the presence of a disease, condition, or microorganism.

props.name: negative finding
props.description: A finding of normality following an examination or investigation looking for the presence of a microorganism, disease, or condition.

props.name: taxonomic classification
props.description: Used for taxonomic or other systematic or hierarchical classification systems.

props.name: assessment scale
props.description: An instrument designed to measure outcomes related to one's medical condition.

props.name: International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective knee evaluation form
props.description: International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective knee evaluation form is a knee-specific measure of symptoms, function, and sports activity.

props.name: Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS)
props.description: A self-administered questionnaire that assesses five outcomes: pain, symptoms, activities of daily living, sport and recreation function, and knee-related quality of life.

props.name: Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score Physical function Short form (KOOS-PS)
props.description: A 7-item measure of physical function derived from the function, daily living and function, sports and recreational activity subscales of the KOOS. It measures people's opinions about the difficulties they experience with activity due to problems with their knee.

props.name: Knee Outcome Survey Activities of Daily Living scale (KOS-ADL)
props.description: A patient-reported instrument for the measurement of functional limitations commonly experienced by individuals with various knee conditions. It has two separate scales: the Activities of Daily Living Scale and the Sports Activity Scale. The Activities of Daily Living Scale includes items related to symptoms and functional limitations experienced during activities of daily living, while the Sports Activity Scale consists of items related to symptoms and functional limitations experienced during sports activities.

props.name: Lysholm knee scoring scale
props.description: Lysholm knee scoring scale is a scoring scale for knee ligament surgery follow-up emphasizing evaluation of symptoms of instability, which is defined as 'giving way' during activity.

props.name: Oxford knee score
props.description: Oxford knee score is a questionnaire for patients having a total knee replacement that reflects their assessment of knee-related health status and benefits of treatment.

props.name: Activity Rating Scale (ARS)
props.description: A self administered rating scale to assess an individual's activity level.

props.name: Tegner Activity Scale (TAS)
props.description: Tegner Activity Scale (TAS) is an activity grading scale, where work and sport activities are graded numerically.

props.name: Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis (WOMAC) score
props.description: Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score Physical function Short form (KOOS-PS) is questionnaire designed to obtain patients' opinions about the difficulties experienced with physical activities due to knee problems.

props.name: modified Cincinnati rating score
props.description: A questionnaire that assesses how knee pain has affected one's ability to manage in everyday life. The original form of the Cincinnati Knee Rating System has multiple parts: symptoms, sports activity, and activities of daily living scales, along with clinical parameters. The modified version requires patient input only and provides the user with an overall score as well as symptom and functional subscores.

props.name: Knee Society clinical rating score
props.description: A rating system for patients undergoing knee arthroplasty that rates only the knee joint itself and a functional score that rates the patient's ability to walk and climb stairs.

Ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy
props.description: Conjugate-gaze palsy is one of the most common eyemovement abnormalities in patients with acute stroke. The eyes may be deviated to one side, either to the side of a hemispheral lesion or to the opposite side of a pons lesion, with gaze paresis towards the opposite side.

props.name: Action tremor
props.description: A tremor present when the limbs are active, either when outstretched in a certain position or throughout a voluntary movement.

props.name: Somnolence
props.description: omnolence (alternatively "sleepiness" or "drowsiness") is a state of strong desire for sleep, or sleeping for unusually long periods (compare hypersomnia).

props.name: Rubral tremor
props.description: Rubral tremor is characterized by a slow coarse tremor at rest that is exacerbated by postural adjustments and by guided voluntary movements.

props.name: Isometric tremor
props.description: An isometric tremor occurs with muscle contraction against a rigid stationary object (e.g., when making a fist).

props.name: Metamorphopsia
props.description: General term for a range of visual perceptual disorders in which the apparent shape, size, outline, color, number, movement, or other physical characteristics of visual objects are distorted.

props.name: Resting tremor
props.description: A resting tremor occurs when muscles are at rest and becomes less noticeable or disappears when the affected muscles are moved. Resting tremors are often slow and coarse.

props.name: Truncal titubation
props.description: Tremor of the trunk in an anterior-posterior plane at 3-4 Hz.

props.name: Head titubation
props.description: A head tremor of moderate speed (3 to 4 Hz) in the anterior-posterior direction.

props.name: Migrainous infarction
props.description: Migraine is a neurological disease associated with an increased stroke risk.

props.name: Transient ischemic attack
props.description: A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is an episode in which neurological symptoms occur as a result of cerebrovascular disease, but resolve completely within 24 h.

props.name: Brain abscess
props.description: Brain abscesses are an intracranial mass of immune cells, pus (i.e., collection of dead neutrophils), and other materials stemming from a bacterial or fungal infection.

props.name: Voice tremor
props.description: A wavering, unsteady voice that reflects involuntary and approximately sinusoidal oscillation of motor unit firings of laryngeal muscles. Vocal tremor results in low frequency modulations of voice frequency or amplitude and intermittent voice instability.

props.name: Postural tremor
props.description: A type of tremors that is triggered by holding a limb in a fixed position.

props.name: Tremor by anatomical site
props.description: Tremor classified by the affected body part.

props.name: Intention tremor
props.description: An oscillatory cerebellar ataxia that tends to be absent when the limbs are inactive and during the first part of voluntary movement but worsening as the movement continues and greater precision is required (e.g., in touching a target such as the patient's nose or a physician's finger).

props.name: Syncope
props.description: Syncope is defined as a short and transient loss of consciousness with loss of postural control. Syncope is rarely caused by TIA or stroke. Among a series of 551 patients with acute cerebrovascular disorders, syncope was observed in 6% of those who had suffered stroke and in less than 1% of those with TIAs, more often in the carotid than in the vertebrobasilar territory. About half of all cases were attributed to seizures, and the rest to brainstem ischemia (with impairment of the ARAS) or to bihemispheric dysfunction related to diaschisis.

props.name: Upper limb postural tremor
props.description: A type of tremors that is triggered by holding an arm in a fixed position.

props.name: Titubation
props.description: Nodding movement of the head or body.

props.name: Kinetic tremor
props.description: Tremor that occurs during any voluntary movement. It may include visually or non-visually guided movements. Tremor during target directed movement is called intention tremor.

props.name: contrast bath
props.description: 将需要治疗的身体部分交替浸入热水与冷水之中，或以热水与冷水交替喷射某一患部进行治疗的方法。

props.name: Artery-to-artery embolism
props.description: Thrombus formation on atherosclerotic plaques may embolize to intracranial arteries producing an artery to artery embolic stroke.

props.name: Matrix metalloproteinase 9
props.description: An endopeptidase that is structurally similar to MATRIX METALLOPROTEINASE 2. It degrades GELATIN types I and V; COLLAGEN TYPE IV; and COLLAGEN TYPE V.

props.name: Inflammatory mediators of secondary brain damage
Microcirculatory dysfunction
props.description: The hypothesis that the cerebral microcirculation has to be involved in posthemorrhagic cerebral ischemia was based on experimental studies showing that acutely following SAH intracranial pressure increased so dramatically that CBF (and in parallel CPP) decrease to almost zero thereby causing global cerebral ischemia.

props.name: Matrix metalloproteinase 2
props.description: A secreted endopeptidase homologous with INTERSTITIAL COLLAGENASE, but which possesses an additional fibronectin-like domain.

props.name: Lipid peroxidation
props.description: Lipid peroxidation can be described generally as a process under which oxidants such as free radicals or nonradical species attack lipids containing carbon-carbon double bond(s), especially polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) that involve hydrogen abstraction from a carbon, with oxygen insertion resulting in lipid peroxyl radicals and hydroperoxides as described previously.

props.name: Vascular thrombosis
props.description: The formation of a blood clot in the lumen of a vessel; causes include coagulation disorders, and vascular endothelial injury.

props.name: Free radical synthesis
props.description: free radical is an especially reactive atom or group of atoms that has one or more unpaired electrons; especially :  one that is produced in the body by natural biological processes or introduced from outside (as in tobacco smoke, toxins, or pollutants) and that can damage cells, proteins, and DNA by altering their chemical structure.  Free radicals cause lipid peroxidation, membrane damage, dysregulation of cellular processes, and mutations of the genome. In fact, reactive oxygen species can damage virtually any cellular component. Cell damage causes aberrations in ion homeostasis, cell signaling, and gene expression.

props.name: Brain tumor
props.description: An abnormal mass of tissue in which some cells (glial or non-glial) grow and multiply uncontrollably. A tumor can be benign or malignant.

props.name: Differential diagnosis
props.description: Differential diagnosis refers to the process of differentiating one diagnosis from another, and in turn, providing the most fitting diagnosis based on an individual’s presentation.

props.name: Magnetic resonance imaging
props.description: Non-invasive method of demonstrating internal anatomy based on the principle that atomic nuclei in a strong magnetic field absorb pulses of radiofrequency energy and emit them as radiowaves which can be reconstructed into computerized images. The concept includes proton spin tomographic techniques.

props.name: Six Minute Walk Test
props.description: The six-minute walk test (6MWT) measures the distance (6MWD) that a person can quickly walk on a flat, hard surface in 6 min. The test is submaximal and self-paced, with rest breaks allowed as needed.

props.name: Evaluation of Atherosclerotic Cerebrovascular Disease
props.description: An overview of the evaluation of patients who present with neurologic symptoms that may be consistent with stroke includes the following:  understanding the classification of stroke, An initial quick evaluation to stabilize vital signs, determine if intracranial hemorrhage is present, and, in patients with ischemic stroke, decide if reperfusion therapy is warranted, Forming a hypothesis of the stroke etiology based upon the history, physical examination, and initial brain imaging study (usually a noncontrast head CT scan) and  Confirming the precise pathophysiologic process with more directed diagnostic testing.

props.name: Epidural bleeding
props.description: Bleeding between the skull and the dura, the thick, outermost layer covering the brain.

props.name: Subdural hemorrhage
props.description: ccumulation of blood in the SUBDURAL SPACE between the DURA MATER and the arachnoidal layer of the MENINGES. This condition primarily occurs over the surface of a CEREBRAL HEMISPHERE, but may develop in the spinal canal (HEMATOMA, SUBDURAL, SPINAL). Subdural hematoma can be classified as the acute or the chronic form, with immediate or delayed symptom onset, respectively. Symptoms may include loss of consciousness, severe HEADACHE, and deteriorating mental status.

props.name: Hypotension
props.description: Occurs when blood pressure is reduced to <= 90/60 mmHg

props.name: Episodic ataxia
props.description: Periodic spells of incoordination and imbalance.

props.name: Multiple sclerosis
props.description: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (CNS) affecting the brain and spinal cord.

props.name: Todds paralysis
props.description: Todd’s paralysis is a brief period of paralysis that occurs in the aftermath of a seizure.

props.name: Hypoglycemia
props.description: Hypoglycemia is characterized by extremely low blood glucose levels. Although 60–70 mg/dL (or milligrams per deciliter) is typically cited as the lower level for normal glucose, different values have also been proposed. Hypoglycemia is commonly associated with, among other symptoms, generalized discomfort, sweating, weakness, irritability, tremor, and poor motor coordination.

props.name: Tau protein
props.description: Tau protein (TP) is a structural microtubule-associated protein that is well known for its association with a variety of neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease.

props.name: CC chemokine receptors
props.description: Chemokine receptors that are specific for CC CHEMOKINES.

props.name: Shoulder pain
props.description: Unilateral or bilateral pain of the shoulder. It is often caused by physical activities such as work or sports participation, but may also be pathologic in origin.

props.name: alpha 2 macroglobulin
props.description: a2-macroglobulin plays a role as a carrier protein for IL‑6, protecting the cytokine from degradative proteases in the plasma.

props.name: Functional comorbidity index
props.description: The FCI was developed as a comorbidity index with physical function as the outcome of interest, using an 18-item (comorbidities) self-administered questionnaire where the FCI score is the sum of the number of conditions reported for the person (0–18).

props.name: Ischemic modified albumin
props.description: Albumin is the most abundant protein found in plasma, functioning as a nonspecific carrier molecule and maintaining oncotic pressure. In the context of ischemia, structural changes occur at the N-terminus of the protein, possibly as a result of exposure to ROS. This change in the albumin protein is detected by a cobalt-binding test. Over the last decade, increased ischemia-modified albumin concentration has been linked to acute myocardial ischemia, limb ischemia, mesenteric ischemia and deep venous thrombosis . Serum levels of ischemia-modified albumin are increased in subjects with both ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke compared with controls at baseline.

props.name: Shwartz Index
props.description: The Shwartz Index consists of 21 weighted conditions and evaluates the negative influence of comorbid conditions on the treatment of the primary condition, including stroke, lung disease, heart disease, prostate disease, low back disorders, and hip fracture.

props.name: Diagnosis cost group
props.description: DCGs were originally developed to predict future costs for Medicare beneficiaries. Each ICD-9-CM code is first grouped into diagnostic clusters of clinically related disorders. Clusters are subsequently grouped into hierarchical condition categories that consider the severity and expected costliness of related disorders. Examples of hierarchies are congestive heart failure and diabetes mellitus with chronic complications. Hierarchies may be further clustered into aggregated condition categories.

props.name: CC chemokine receptor 2
props.description: CCR receptors with specificity for CHEMOKINE CCL2 and several other CCL2-related chemokines. They are expressed at high levels in T-LYMPHOCYTES; B-LYMPHOCYTES; MACROPHAGES; BASOPHILS; and NK CELLS.

props.name: Obesity
props.description: A status with BODY WEIGHT that is grossly above the acceptable or desirable weight, usually due to accumulation of excess FATS in the body. The standards may vary with age, sex, genetic or cultural background. In the BODY MASS INDEX, a BMI greater than 30.0 kg/m2 is considered obese, and a BMI greater than 40.0 kg/m2 is considered morbidly obese (MORBID OBESITY).

props.name: Measures of comorbidity
props.description: In epidemiology, a rating scale for comorbidity.

props.name: Prior stroke
props.description: prior stroke is a strong predisposing risk factor for new stroke and is the most common disease with ICH.

props.name: Constipation
props.description: Constipation is recognized as a serious problem in clinical practice, affecting 60% of those in stroke rehabilitation wards.

props.name: Gastritis
props.description: Inflammation of the GASTRIC MUCOSA, a lesion observed in a number of unrelated disorders.

props.name: Limb ataxia
props.description: A kind of `ataxia` (HP:0001251) that affects movements of the extremities.

props.name: Dysmetria
props.description: A type of `ataxia` (HP:0001251) characterized by the inability to carry out movements with the correct range and motion across the plane of more than one joint related to incorrect estimation of the distances required for targeted movements.

props.name: Truncal ataxia
props.description: A kind of `ataxia` (HP:0001251) that affects the proximal musculature, especially that involved in gait stability.

props.name: Limb dysmetria
props.description: A type of `dysmetria` (HP:0001310) involving the limbs.

props.name: Dysdiadochokinesis
props.description: A type of `ataxia` (HP:0001251) characterized by the impairment of the ability to perform rapidly alternating movements, such as rhythmically tapping the fingers on the knee, generally related to a cerebellar lesion.

props.name: Cytotoxic edema
props.description: Cytotoxic edema is defined as the premorbid cellular process, otherwise known as cellular edema, oncotic cell swelling, or oncosis, whereby extracellular Na+ and other cations enter into neurons and astrocytes and accumulate intracellularly, in part due to failure of energy-dependent mechanisms of extrusion.

props.name: Cell death
props.description: Any biological process that results in permanent cessation of all vital functions of a cell. A cell should be considered dead when any one of the following molecular or morphological criteria is met: (1) the cell has lost the integrity of its plasma membrane; (2) the cell, including its nucleus, has undergone complete fragmentation into discrete bodies (frequently referred to as "apoptotic bodies"); and/or (3) its corpse (or its fragments) have been engulfed by an adjacent cell in vivo.

props.name: Interleukin 10
props.description: IL-10 is a major anti-inflammatory molecule in various organ injuries. It is produced by infiltrating immune cells and reactive glial cells after ischemic brain injury. Viral overexpression of IL-10 in ischemic brain is neuroprotective.

props.name: heat therapy
props.description: 以各种热源为介质，将热直接传作用于人体治疗疾病的方法

props.name: cryotherapy
props.description: 以寒冷作用于皮肤或黏膜以治疗疾病的方法。

props.name: FLAIR weighted images
props.description: A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pulse sequence that uses an inversion recovery technique to null fluids present in the imaging area, improving clarity of the object of interest.

props.name: N acetylaspartate
props.description: N-acetylaspartate (NAA) is a free amino acid representing approximately 1% of the dry weight of the brain.

props.name: N terminal proBNP
props.description: A bioassay to determine an individual’s level of N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP).

props.name: Spastic dysarthria
props.description: A type of dysarthria related to bilateral damage of the upper motor neuron tracts of the pyramidal and extra- pyramidal tracts. Speech of affected individuals is slow, effortful, and has a harsh vocal quality.

props.name: Cervical artery dissection
props.description: Arterial dissection is an uncommon vascular wall condition that typically involves a tear at some point in the artery's lining and the formation of an intimal flap, which allows blood to penetrate into the muscular portion of the vessel wall.

props.name: Glutamate binds to N methyl D aspartate receptor
Nasal, dysarthic speech
props.description: Speech impairment due to neuropathy, speech-related muscle paralysis, decreased contractility, or lack of motor coordination

props.name: Thrombosis
props.description: Thrombosis is a critical event in the arterial diseases associated with myocardial infarction and stroke, and venous thromboembolic disorders account for considerable morbidity and mortality.

props.name: Paraoxonase 1
props.description: An enzyme which catalyzes the hydrolysis of an aryl-dialkyl phosphate to form dialkyl phosphate and an aryl alcohol. It can hydrolyze a broad spectrum of organophosphate substrates and a number of aromatic carboxylic acid esters. It may also mediate an enzymatic protection of LOW DENSITY LIPOPROTEINS against oxidative modification and the consequent series of events leading to ATHEROMA formation. The enzyme was previously regarded to be identical with Arylesterase (EC 3.1.1.2).

props.name: Glutathione S transferase P
props.description: A transferase that catalyzes the addition of aliphatic, aromatic, or heterocyclic FREE RADICALS as well as EPOXIDES and arene oxides to GLUTATHIONE. Addition takes place at the SULFUR. It also catalyzes the reduction of polyol nitrate by glutathione to polyol and nitrite.

props.name: Tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases
props.description: A family of secreted protease inhibitory proteins that regulates the activity of SECRETED MATRIX METALLOENDOPEPTIDASES. They play an important role in modulating the proteolysis of EXTRACELLULAR MATRIX, most notably during tissue remodeling and inflammatory processes.

props.name: B-type natriuretic peptide
props.description: A PEPTIDE that is secreted by the BRAIN and the HEART ATRIA, stored mainly in cardiac ventricular MYOCARDIUM. It can cause NATRIURESIS; DIURESIS; VASODILATION; and inhibits secretion of RENIN and ALDOSTERONE. It improves heart function. It contains 32 AMINO ACIDS.

props.name: PARK 7
props.description: A protein that is a translation product of the human PARK7 gene or a 1:1 ortholog thereof.

props.name: Ephedrine
props.description: Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic amine and substituted amphetamine commonly used as a stimulant, concentration aid, decongestant, appetite suppressant, and to treat hypotension associated with anaesthesia.

props.name: Antiphospholipid syndrome
props.description: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is defined by the development of thrombosis and/or adverse obstetric events in the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL).

props.name: Carotid artery dissection
props.description: Dissection of the carotid artery in the neck is a relatively common condition. Most dissections are spontaneous, likely related to activities that cause sudden stretch of the pharyngeal portion of the carotid artery. Carotid artery dissection is a separation of the layers of the artery wall supplying oxygen-bearing blood to the head and brain and is the most common cause of stroke in young adults.

props.name: Granulomatous angitis of central nervous system
Ocular dyssynergia
props.description: A type of `dyssynergia` (HP:0010867) affecting eye movements and characterized by the inability to smoothly follow a visual target across the visual field.

props.name: Dyssynergia
props.description: A type of `ataxia` (HP:0001251) characterized by the impairment of the ability to smoothly perform the elements of a voluntary movement in the appropriate order and speed. With dyssynergia, a voluntary movement appears broken down into its component parts.

props.name: N glycan
props.description: N-glycans are oligosaccharide structures covalently linked (sugar–amino acid linkage) to an asparagine residue of a protein in a consensus sequence (GlcNAc-b-Asn). These sugar structures are highly heterogeneous and their biosynthesis is closely linked to the cellular metabolism, thereby they reflect the metabolic status of cells.

props.name: Abasia
props.description: A severe form of gait ataxia such that an affected person cannot walk at all.

props.name: Gait ataxia
props.description: A type of `ataxia` (HP:0001251) characterized by the impairment of the ability to coordinate the movements required for normal walking.

props.name: Asynergia
props.description: A type of `dyssynergy` (HP:0010867) characterized by the lack of the ability to smoothly perform the elements of a voluntary movement in the appropriate order and speed.

props.name: Cerebellar ataxia associated with quadrupedal gait
props.description: The presence of cerebellar signs and symptoms such as lack of balance associated with quadrupedal gait (locomotion on all four extremities with a 'bear-like' gait with the legs held straight).

props.name: Progressive gait ataxia
props.description: A type of `gait ataxia` (HP:0002066) displaying progression of clinical severity.

props.name: Dabigatran
props.description: Dabigatran etexilate is the orally administered prodrug and is rapidly converted by tissue esterases to dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor. When taken by mouth, the bioavailability of dabigatran is approximately 7%.

props.name: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
props.description: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) is a rare and potentially deadly condition. Common etiologies include hypercoagulable diseases, low flow states, dehydration, adjacent infectious processes, oral contraceptives, hormonal replacement therapy, pregnancy, and puerperium. Symptoms include nausea, seizures, severe focal neurological deficits, coma, and headache (the most common presenting symptom).

props.name: prudent diet
props.description: A  prudent  diet,  characterised  by  high  intakes  of  fruits, vegetables,   legumes,   ﬁ sh,   and   whole   grains,   was associated  with  a  lower  risk  of  stroke  after  14  years  of follow-up  of  71 768  women  (relative  risk  0·78,  95%  CI  0·61–1·01;   comparing   extreme   quintiles)   whereas   a western  diet,  characterised  by  high  intakes  of  red  and processed meats, reﬁ ned grains, and sweets and desserts, was associated with an increased risk of stroke (relative risk 1·58, 95% CI 1·15–2·15; comparing the highest with lowest quintiles of the western diet).

props.name: sport
props.description: For patients with ischemic stroke or TIA who are capable of engaging in physical activity, at least 3 to 4 sessions per week of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic physical exercise are reasonable to reduce stroke risk factors. Sessions should last an average of 40 minutes.

props.name: Interleukin 6
props.description: A cytokine that stimulates the growth and differentiation of B-LYMPHOCYTES and is also a growth factor for HYBRIDOMAS and plasmacytomas. It is produced by many different cells including T-LYMPHOCYTES; MONOCYTES; and FIBROBLASTS.

props.name: Angioplasty
props.description: Balloon angioplasty with or without stent placement represents a different approach to the recanalization of arterial occlusion. This strategy, which is similar to the approach commonly taken in patients with acute myocardial infarction, was hampered for a long time by the absence of dedicated catheters for the cerebral vasculature.

props.name: High potassium intake
props.description: higher level of potassium intake has been associated with a reduced risk of stroke in prospective studies. The  recommended  potassium intake >4.7 g/d (120 mmol/d).

props.name: Antioxidants
props.description: Naturally occurring or synthetic substances that inhibit or retard oxidation reactions. They counteract the damaging effects of oxidation in animal tissues.

props.name: Edoxaban
props.description: Edoxaban, an oral direct factor Xa inhibitor, has been found non-inferior to warfarin for preventing stroke and systemic embolism in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF), with a lower rate of intracranial bleeding.

props.name: Elevation of intracellular Ca 2 pluse level
Pathophysiology of Atherosclerotic cerebrovascular disease
props.description: The pathophysiology of any disease is how the normal physiology is altered by a disease, or pathologic, process.

props.name: Atrial fibrillation
props.description: The most common cause of embolism occurs in a heart (cardiac) condition called ‘‘atrial fibrillation.’’ Normally, each electrical impulse causes the atria (upper chambers of the heart) to beat in a strong, coordinated, and efficient manner. The blood flows smoothly. In atrial fibrillation, there are no coordinated electrical impulses, and therefore there is no coordinated mechanical pumping of blood in the atria. When this occurs over long periods of time (usually weeks to months or even longer), clots form in these upper chambers of the heart.

props.name: Matrix metalloproteinase 13
props.description: A secreted matrix metalloproteinase that plays a physiological role in the degradation of extracellular matrix found in skeletal tissues. It is synthesized as an inactive precursor that is activated by the proteolytic cleavage of its N-terminal propeptide.

props.name: Dipyridamole with aspirin
props.description: The combination of extended-release dipyridamole and aspirin reduces the relative risk of stroke, death, and myocardial infarction (MI). It is used for the secondary prevention of ischemic stroke and TIAs.

props.name: Tumor necrosis factor alpha
props.description: Serum glycoprotein produced by activated MACROPHAGES and other mammalian MONONUCLEAR LEUKOCYTES. It has necrotizing activity against tumor cell lines and increases ability to reject tumor transplants. Also known as TNF-alpha, it is only 30% homologous to TNF-beta (LYMPHOTOXIN), but they share TNF RECEPTORS.

props.name: Fruit
props.description: The fleshy or dry ripened ovary of a plant, enclosing the seed or seeds.

props.name: Vitamin E intake
props.description: Vitamin E is a lipid-soluble antioxidant that increases the resistance   of   LDL   cholesterol   to   oxidation,   reduces proliferation   of   smooth   muscle   cells,   and   reduces adhesiveness   of   platelets   to   collagen.   This   vitamin inhibits lipid peroxidation by scavenging reactive oxygen species and preserving cell membranes.

props.name: Low molecular weight heparins
props.description: Low molecular weight heparins (LMWH) have been shown to have advantages over standard unfractionated heparins in the prevention of pulmonary embolism and, in this context, appear to have a better safety profile. There was, therefore, considerable hope that they would prove more efficacious in the treatment of acute stroke.

props.name: Eyelid apraxia
props.description: Eyelid apraxia is manifested as involuntary levator muscle suppression and orbicularis oculi muscle inhibition. It is one of the typical signs of Parkinson's disease in the elderly.

props.name: Limb apraxia
props.description: Difficulty in performing the correct execution of limbs movements in absence of motor impairment.

props.name: Speech apraxia
props.description: A type of apraxia that is characterized by difficulty or inability to execute speech movements because of problems with coordination and motor problems, leading to incorrect articulation. An increase of errors with increasing word and phrase length may occur.

props.name: Oculomotor apraxia
props.description: Inability to follow objects visually with compensatory head movements, decreased smooth pursuit, and cancellation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex.

props.name: Lipohyalinosis
props.description: Lipohyalinosis is a small-vessel disease in the brain. Originally defined by Fisher as 'segmental arteriolar wall disorganisation', it is characterised by vessel wall thickening and a resultant reduction in luminal diameter. Fisher considered this small-vessel disease to be the result of hypertension, induced in the acute stage by fibrinoid necrosis that would lead to occlusion and hence lacunar stroke.

props.name: Gait apraxia
props.description: Gait apraxia affecting the ability to make walking movements with the legs.

props.name: Cocaine hydrochloride
props.description: Cocaine is a naturally occurring chemical found in the leaves of Erythroxylum coca or coca plant, which is native to South America. Coca leaves have been used and abused for hundreds of years. Cocaine is a highly addictive stimulant drug that directly affects the nervous system, including the brain.

props.name: Inflammatory disorder
props.description: Inflammatory abnormalities are a large group of disorders that underlie a vast variety of human diseases. The immune system is often involved with inflammatory disorders, demonstrated in both allergic reactions and some myopathies, with many immune system disorders resulting in abnormal inflammation. Non-immune diseases with etiological origins in inflammatory processes include cancer, atherosclerosis, and ischaemic heart disease.

props.name: Rice intake
props.description: Rice consumption has been associated with an increased risk of stroke.

props.name: Aspirin
props.description: Aspirin blocks prostaglandin synthetase action, which in turn inhibits prostaglandin synthesis and prevents the formation of platelet-aggregating thromboxane A2.

props.name: Vegetable
props.description: cruciferous and green leafy vegetables (e.g. cabbages, turnips, broccoli), together with citrus fruit and juice, protected against stroke.

props.name: Scavenger Receptors, Class A
props.description: A family of scavenger receptors that mediate the influx of LIPIDS into MACROPHAGES and are involved in FOAM CELL formation.
